item.title: How to Make a Kakuro Puzzle From Scratch
item.description: You’ve solved a few hundred Kakuro grids, and one evening you decide to make one. Graph paper, a pencil, an hour. You shade some black squares, write digits in the white ones, add up the sums, and hand the finished puzzle to a friend. Ten minutes later they slide it back across the table. The four cells at the bottom of the grid work as 9 8 over 8 9, and they also work as 8 9 over 9 8. Every clue checks out both ways.

item.title: The Ultimate Guide to Advanced Kakuro Tactics
item.description:
The Kakuro book said “Expert.” You believed it for the first ten minutes, while the corners filled in nicely. Now you’re looking at a block in the middle of the grid where every clue has five ways to be right, your pencil marks are three deep, and the eraser has worn a soft gray patch into the paper. You’re one bad decision away from picking a digit and hoping.

You don’t need to be better at arithmetic. Expert Kakuro grids are built to resist the tools that got you through the medium ones, so you need a few more tools. There are four of them, and each one picks up where the last runs out: magic blocks give you a starting point, intersections turn candidates into digits, the 45 rule opens blocks with no starting point, and parity and forcing chains settle the corners where everything else stalls.

item.title: The Complete Beginner's Guide to Solving Kakuro
item.description: Your first Kakuro grid looks like a crossword someone forgot to finish. Black squares are slashed with diagonal lines, small numbers sit in their corners, and rows of empty white boxes wait for you. You pick the first clue you see, a 15 across three cells, and start trying combinations. 9, 5, 1? 8, 4, 3? 7, 6, 2? Ten minutes later your eraser has worn a shiny patch into the paper and you haven’t committed a single digit.

item.title: Designing a Kakuro Grid: Symmetry, Runs and Black Cells
item.description:
You shade black squares on a fresh sheet of graph paper, aiming for something that looks like a real Kakuro grid. Halfway through filling in digits you notice three problems. A white cell in the corner has a down clue but nothing across. One row runs ten cells long. And a little 2x2 pocket in the lower left doesn’t touch anything else.

None of those can be fixed with better digits. The layout was broken before you wrote a single number.

item.title: Essential Magic Blocks: The Kakuro Cheat Sheet
item.description:
You’re twenty minutes into a hard Kakuro, and you’ve just worked out 17 in two cells for the third time tonight. 9 and 8. You knew that. You also knew it the last two times, and you still ran the arithmetic, because the habit hasn’t moved from your head to your eyes yet.

That small tax adds up. Every sum you recompute is attention you don’t spend on the part of the grid that’s hard. Solvers who move fast on expert grids aren’t doing faster mental math. They’ve stopped doing math for a short list of clues, because those clues have exactly one answer and they recognize them on sight.

item.title: Understanding Kakuro Rules and Grid Mechanics
item.description: You open the puzzle book to the Kakuro page, uncap the pen, and look at the first clue cell. It holds two numbers, 24 and 16, separated by a diagonal line. Which one goes with the row? You pick the 24, spend five minutes building a combination that adds up to it across two cells, and realize two cells can’t add up to more than 17. The math was fine. You just solved the wrong clue.

item.title: How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution
item.description: Your first Kakuro is finished. The sums are clean, the layout is symmetric, and every run adds up. Your test solver works through the grid and stops near the bottom. Four cells: 9 and 8 on top, 8 and 9 underneath. Or 8 and 9 on top, 9 and 8 underneath. Every clue checks out both ways. One of the runs through those cells is a 17 in two cells, which you’d have sworn locked them down.

item.title: Mastering the 45 Rule in Kakuro
item.description:
You’ve hit a wall in an expert Kakuro. Every magic block on the page is filled in, every easy crossing is done, and a fat block of empty cells is sitting in the middle of the grid. Each clue around it has five or six workable combinations. You pencil a few, erase them, and pencil them again.

If you’ve played Killer Sudoku, your hand goes to the 45 rule. Every 3×3 box holds 1 through 9, so add up the cages, subtract from 45, and the missing cell falls out. You try it here, and you get 13 for a single cell.

item.title: Kakuro Unique Sums: The Magic of 3, 4, 16, and 17
item.description: A fresh Kakuro grid sits in front of you, every white cell empty. Your eye lands on a 27 running across five cells, so you start there. 9, 8, 6, 3, 1? 9, 7, 5, 4, 2? 8, 7, 6, 4, 2? All valid. There are eleven different digit sets that add to 27 in five cells, and nothing yet tells you which one is right. You pencil in a few, erase them, and start to wonder whether everyone else is just better at math.

item.title: How to Set Kakuro Difficulty: Technique, Not Grid Size
item.description:
The cover says “Extreme Kakuro.” You open to a 15x15 grid and finish it in twelve minutes, because every corner has a 3 or a 17 in two cells that practically fills itself in. Two pages later there’s a little 7x7 marked “Medium.” Forty minutes in, you’re staring at a block of empty cells with no idea where to start.

The labels aren’t lying on purpose. They’re measuring the wrong thing. Big grids take longer; they aren’t necessarily harder. What makes a Kakuro hard is the toughest step the solver is forced to make, and that’s something you choose when you build the puzzle. This article sets out a four-tier grading scale, shows what each level looks like on the page, grades the series 7x7 grid, and then refills the same layout so it needs a deduction one tier harder.

item.title: Intersection Logic: Cross-Referencing Kakuro Clues
item.description: You’ve spotted the 16 in the corner of a Kakuro grid. Two cells, so it’s 7 and 9. You pencil “7 9” into both cells and feel good about it for about four seconds. Then you notice the 17 next to it is “8 9” in both cells too, and the 24 below is “7 8 9” in all three, and the top corner of the grid now looks like a phone keypad.

item.title: How to Cross-Reference Intersecting Kakuro Clues
item.description:
You found the 3 in the corner of your Kakuro grid. Two cells, so it’s a 1 and a 2. You penciled both digits into both cells and felt good about it. Now you’re staring at those two cells, pencil hovering, and the question is simple: which one gets the 1?

You could flip a coin. Half the time you’d be right, and the other half you’d find out fifteen moves later, when a sum on the far side of the grid comes up one short. Knowing which digits belong in an entry is only half the work. The other half is knowing where each one goes, and the answer is almost never in the clue you’re staring at. It’s in the clue that crosses it.

item.title: Build a Kakuro Solver and Generator in Python
item.description:
You write the obvious Kakuro solver first: try 1 through 9 in each empty cell, and back up whenever a sum goes wrong. The series 7x7 grid has 24 white cells. Trying every digit in every cell is 9²⁴ combinations, about 8 × 10²², and your laptop’s fan has opinions about that.

The fix isn’t a faster computer. It’s using what Kakuro already tells you. A clue of 6 over three cells doesn’t allow 729 possibilities. It allows exactly one set of digits, {1, 2, 3}, in some order. Build the solver around the sets each clue allows and the search shrinks to almost nothing.

item.title: Eliminating Guesswork in Kakuro: Parity and Logic
item.description:
You’re down to the last four squares of an expert Kakuro. You try one fill and every clue checks out. You erase it, try the other, and every clue checks out again. Your pencil hovers. One of them has to be wrong, and the puzzle has stopped giving you hints.

So you pick one. If you’re lucky, the grid finishes and you feel nothing. If you’re not, you find out eleven moves later, and now you can’t tell which of those eleven moves to undo.

item.title: Common Kakuro Mistakes Beginners Make and How to Avoid Them
item.description:
Twenty minutes in, the grid is mostly full. You write the last digit of a long across entry, add it up to check, and come up one short. You check the down entry through that cell. It’s off too. You start tracing backward, cell by cell, and the trail keeps going. Ten minutes later you’re erasing half the board and the paper is starting to pill.

Kakuro doesn’t forgive mistakes. Every white cell belongs to two entries, so one wrong digit bends two sums, which bend four more, and the error spreads quietly until something finally refuses to add up, often far from where it started. Almost every ruined grid traces back to one of a few habits, and every one of them can be fixed.

item.title: Designing Kakuro Grids That Hide an Answer
item.description: You want a Kakuro that opens a padlock. The lock takes three digits, and the plan is simple: solve the grid, read three shaded cells, turn the dials. Then you try it. You fill the grid first, shade three cells that happen to look nice, and read off 3-8-6. The lock was set to 4-0-7 weeks ago. Your grid gave you whatever digits the fill happened to produce, and no Kakuro cell can ever hold a 0 anyway.

item.title: Transitioning from Sudoku to Kakuro: What Changes?
item.description:
You can finish a hard Sudoku in ten minutes. You spot X-wings without trying, and naked pairs jump out at you. So you flip to the Kakuro page expecting a warm-up, and twenty minutes later you’ve placed four digits, erased three of them, and you’re refusing to write a 5 in a cell because there’s already a 5 further along the row.

That 5 is legal, by the way. You aren’t bad at Kakuro. You’re running Sudoku instincts on a puzzle that only looks similar. Both use the digits 1 through 9, both ban repeats, and both are solved with pencil marks and pure deduction. But the rules underneath work differently, and a few of your best Sudoku habits will steer you wrong.
